paras: The castration of Eli McKnight was a mob attack on a Black man near Gurdon station, Arkansas, on the night of Tuesday, July 25, 1882. Accused of trying to rape Miss Baker, a young woman of the neighborhood, he was captured that evening and castrated by a mob, and a Little Rock Gazette dispatch reported that he would recover. The story spread by wire to papers from Tennessee to Pennsylvania and Washington, D.C., often under headlines that treated the mutilation as a deserved punishment.

According to the Gazette's Arkadelphia correspondent, the accused man, described as "a mulatto, about 26 years of age," went to the house of a Mr. Baker near Gurdon station on Tuesday and found Baker's daughter alone. The dispatch said he assaulted her "with intent to outrage her person," but that her screams brought a house dog to her rescue and she escaped to where her father was working some distance from the house. The shorter wire version gave the same account in one sentence, saying he "was prevented by a house-dog coming to her rescue."

The man was "captured in the evening," though the dispatch did not say by whom. Early that night, according to the same report, "an unknown party forcibly took him into their custody and castrated him." Wire versions said simply that he "was captured by a mob and castrated." None of the reports gave the size of the mob, the names of its members, or the place where the castration was done.

The Gazette special reported that "the negro will recover" and that the sentiment of the community justified "the act of the mob." No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry, or any account from the injured man or other Black residents appears in the coverage.

All of the coverage traces to a single special telegram to the Little Rock Gazette from Arkadelphia, dated July 27, which the National Republican credited by name. The Memphis Public Ledger printed the fullest text under the headline "A Villain's Punishment," calling him "this brute of a negro" and endorsing the mob as men "who had daughters or sisters with innocence to protect." The Memphis Daily Appeal ran the condensed version as "A Would-be Ravisher Mutilated," and the Washington National Republican as "They Castrated Him," both on July 28.

Reprints followed in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer's crime roundup on July 31 and the Jackson Weekly Clarion's news column on August 2. The Union, South Carolina, Weekly Union Times headed its item "An Outrage Avenged" and replaced the word castrated with "suitably punished," while the Stephens City Star said he was "mutilated." Every version stated the accusation as fact, and none questioned the mob's act.
The papers disagreed on names: the wire gave the man as Eli or Ellis McKnight and the place as Gordon or Garden Station, while the fuller Gazette text gave "Eli McKinzy" and "Gurdon station."

reader.title: Castration of Eli McKnight
bases: A mob or 'unknown party' seized a Black man accused of attempted rape and castrated him; he was reported as expected to recover, and no report says he was killed or that his killing was threatened (A1, A4).

Every report traces to one Little Rock Gazette special from Arkadelphia dated July 27 (A2, A4), reprinted in shorter wire form (A1, A3); no independent local account, follow-up or second source was found.

accounts.label: Little Rock Gazette special from Arkadelphia
accounts.gist: McKinzy assaulted Miss Baker alone at home; a dog drove him off; he was captured that evening and an 'unknown party' castrated him early that night; he would recover and the community approved.

accounts.label: Condensed wire report
accounts.gist: A 'burly negro' who tried to outrage Miss Baker but was stopped by a house dog was 'captured by a mob and castrated' near Gordon/Garden Station.

framing.detail: The Gazette special, headed 'A Villain's Punishment' in the Memphis Public Ledger, called him a 'villain' and 'this brute of a negro' and said community sentiment justified the mob.
Memphis Appeal and National Republican ran the short wire under 'A Would-be Ravisher Mutilated' and 'They Castrated Him', stating the accusation as fact.
The Union Times headed the reprint 'An Outrage Avenged' and said he was 'suitably punished'.

conflicts.note: A4 prints the fuller original special and may be closer to the source; the wire condensation gave McKnight.
All three appear to be renderings of the same station name in the same dispatch; A4 is the fullest text.
Not a substantive disagreement; A4 also calls it 'the mob'.
